problem: Traditional document chunking in retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) fragments context, leading to incomplete information retrieval and diminished generation coherence (p.1, p.2). The comparative strengths and limitations of advanced alternatives such as late chunking and contextual retrieval remain unclear in integrated RAG workflows (p.1, p.3).
methodology: The study conducts a rigorous comparative analysis of late chunking, traditional early chunking, and contextual retrieval within a unified setup (p.2, p.3). For contextual retrieval, the method incorporates contextualization using Microsoft's Phi-3.5-mini-instruct, a weighted rank fusion strategy combining dense embeddings with sparse BM25 vectors, and a Jina Reranker V2 Base model (p.8, p.9). For late chunking, the document is embedded at the token level first and then segmented into chunks using boundary cues with mean pooling (p.4).
dataset: Experiments utilize the NFCorpus dataset (tested on the full dataset for RQ#1 and a 20% subset for RQ#2 due to GPU memory constraints) and the MSMarco dataset (p.7).
results: ContextualRankFusion generally obtains better overall retrieval results compared to late chunking on the tested NFCorpus subset, but requires significantly greater computational resources and VRAM (p.10, p.11, Table 5). Late chunking does not consistently outperform early chunking across all models and datasets, as demonstrated by the superior performance of the early version with BGE-M3 on NFCorpus and Stella-V5 on MSMarco (p.10, p.12, Tables 3 and 4).
key_findings: Contextual retrieval preserves semantic coherence more effectively through chunk contextualization, rank fusion, and reranking, but demands greater computational resources (p.1, p.10, p.12). Late chunking offers higher computational efficiency by leveraging embedding models without additional training, but tends to sacrifice relevance and completeness in certain settings (p.1, p.12).
limitations: Neither technique offers a definitive solution, as performance varies depending on the chosen dataset, model, and document length (p.2, p.12). Contextual retrieval requires high VRAM usage (around 20GB), which limits batch sizes and slows generation times, while dynamic segmenting models are generative and can lead to inconsistencies in wording (p.7, p.11).
title: Reconstructing Context
